subject: english-literature

moments.title: Donne's early career
moments.who: John Donne, Inns of Court and London courts
moments.body: Donne (c. 1572-1631) studied at Oxford, the Inns of Court. He converted from Catholic to Anglican. His early secular love poetry — Songs and Sonnets — was circulated in manuscript. Marriage to Anne More (1601) cost him his court career.
moments.takeaway: Donne's poetry circulated in manuscript during his life and wasn't published until 1633, two years after his death.

moments.title: Donne ordained
moments.who: Donne as Dean of St Paul's
moments.body: Donne was ordained 1615 and became Dean of St Paul's in 1621. His sermons (Donne preached over 160) became some of the most celebrated of the period. His Holy Sonnets and Divine Poems date partly from this period.
moments.takeaway: Donne's 'Devotions upon Emergent Occasions' (1624) included 'No man is an island' and 'Ask not for whom the bell tolls' — phrases that have entered English culture.

moments.title: T.S. Eliot's revival
moments.body: 1921: T.S. Eliot's essay 'The Metaphysical Poets' (review of Grierson's anthology) revives interest in Donne and his contemporaries. The 'dissociation of sensibility' thesis argues English poetry lost its capacity for unified thought-feeling after the metaphysicals.
moments.takeaway: Modernist criticism reshaped which 17th-century poets were considered important. Donne moved from being a minor figure to a central one.

now.title: Metaphysical wit
now.body: Donne is now firmly canonical. Modern editions (Helen Gardner's Divine Poems, John Carey's biography, Achsah Guibbory's recent work) sustain serious scholarship. Modern readers find the combination of intellectual wit and emotional intensity attractive.
now.open_questions: Was the 'dissociation of sensibility' real? Eliot's thesis has been substantially criticised. The mid-17th-century English Civil War and the rise of Lockean empiricism are real changes; whether they damaged poetry's capacities is debated.

reflection: A poet whose work circulated in manuscript during his lifetime became, three centuries later, a canonical English poet thanks to T.S. Eliot's modernist revival. Donne's combination of metaphysical wit, sexual frankness and religious intensity speaks to modern readers across the gap.
